newsitem.title: UK: Deutsche Telekom bodes well for France, Italy.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom bodes well for France, Italy.

text.p: A feverish debut of the first tranche of German Telekom, which was five times oversubscribed, should bode well for France and Italy as their national phone monopolies head for a full sell-off, analysts said on Monday.
The offering is likely to be watched closely not only by investors but by other European governments anxious to unload state telecom monopolies.

As newly-floated shares in Germany's phone giant, Europe's largest-ever initial public offering, surged 20 percent before dipping amid profit-taking, analysts said potential investors in France Telecom and Italy's STET should take heed.

"Deutsche Telekom has obviously given people encouragement that these deals are firstly absorbable, and secondly, that there's good appetite for them," said James Golob, telecoms analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

France Telecom is France's most profitable company. The government is expected to float an initial 25 percent tranche in April. Also on the auction block is Italian telecommunications company Societa Finanziaria Telefonica PA (STET).
STET is already partially floated -- but a full sell-off is due in late 1997.

Analysts said that many observers had underestimated the strength of retail demand for Deutsche Telekom, which alone covered the 713 million share issue -- despite an eleventh-hour 20 percent increase in the issue size.

The price for the monster issue was fixed at the high end of the range of 25 to 30 marks that was indicated a month ago by the company, following huge interest shown in the offering both in Germany and abroad.

German investors took two thirds of the $13 billion issue, with the remainder going abroad. The shares opened at 33.20 marks, a robust premium to their 29.50 mark issue price, and rose as high as 34.10 marks as traders scrambled to buy stock.
Institutions, thwarted from receiving stock they had asked for amid rampant retail demand, were forced into the open market to buy shares at premium.

Deutsche Telekom's offering marks not only the partial sale of the world's third-largest telecoms group in terms of turnover, but it represents a huge effort to get traditionally reluctant small investors involved in the stock market.
And both Italian and French markets have much greater experience of retail demand for equities.
"Retail and domestic demand have always been very important in terms of all the successful European privatisations," noted one analyst.
"But particularly in respect to Germany, people had always been very gloomy about how much you could realistically expect from retail. Everyone always said they don't buy equities."
The high debt levels of some telecoms groups should not put off investors because of their stable and predictable businesses, noted some analysts.
One broker said he was forecasting a 36 percent compound net income growth for Deutsche Telekom over the next five years.
